card: Paper card. System: high-entropy intermetallics (HEIs). Processing: various methods, including melt-spinning, de-alloying, Joule heating, wet-chemistry, chemical co-reduction, and impregnation. Findings: HeIs have several advantages over disordered high-entropy alloys, including greater structural/thermal stability, more facile site isolation, and more precise control of electronic structures; HeIs provide a number of new ordered alloys; HeIs have been found to have a unique catalytic performance that dramatically exceeds those of conventional catalysts; HeIs can be used for thermal catalysis, including non-oxidative and oxidative dehydrogenation of propane; HeIs can be used for electrocatalysis, including oxygen reduction reaction (ORR); HeIs can exhibit multifunctional effects, including synergetic contributions of element-specific functions. Mechanism: The combination of the enthalpic and entropic effects in HEIs significantly improves the thermodynamic stability. Limitations: The catalysis field of HEIs is in the preliminary stage, and it lacks basic information. Future work: Conducting more remarkable and deeper studies is urgently necessary to open a new paradigm in HEI catalysis. Quote: "The combination of the enthalpic and entropic effects in HEIs significantly improves the thermodynamic stability"

Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy intermetallics (HEIs) be used as catalysts for various reactions, including propylene production, acetylene semihydrogenation, hydrogen evolution reaction, oxygen reduction reaction, and alcohol oxidation?. System: High-entropy intermetallics (HEIs) with various compositions, such as (PtCoCu)(GeGaSn), (PtCoNi)(SnInGa), (NiFeCu)(GaGe), and (FeCoNi)3(TiAl). Test conditions: Various reactions, including propylene production, acetylene semihydrogenation, hydrogen evolution reaction, oxygen reduction reaction, and alcohol oxidation, under different conditions, such as temperature, pressure, and electrolyte. Findings: HEIs exhibit high catalytic activity and stability for various reactions; HEIs can be designed to have specific properties, such as site isolation and electronic structure, to enhance catalytic performance; HEIs show improved durability and resistance to degradation compared to traditional catalysts; HEIs can be used for various reactions, including propylene production, acetylene semihydrogenation, hydrogen evolution reaction, oxygen reduction reaction, and alcohol oxidation; HEIs exhibit high mass activity and low overpotential for hydrogen evolution reaction and oxygen reduction reaction. Mechanism: The authors propose that the high catalytic activity of HEIs is due to the site isolation effect, electronic structure, and synergistic contribution of multiple elements. Limitations: The authors mention that the synthesis of HEIs can be challenging and that further understanding of the structural and compositional changes of HEIs at the atomic level is necessary. Future work: The authors suggest that establishing an easy, simple, and cost-effective procedure for the synthesis of HEI catalysts with high homogeneity and size control is highly desired. Quote: "the emergence of HEIs demonstrates that we are moving toward the cherished goal in alloy catalysis"

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanocatalysts be synthesized to achieve simultaneous high performance for both hydrogen evolution (HER) and methanol oxidation (MOR) reactions, and what is the mechanism behind their enhanced activity and stability?. System: Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27 high-entropy alloy nanoparticles supported on carbon (Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C). Processing: One-pot oil phase synthesis at 220 °C for 2 hours at atmospheric pressure using metal acetylacetonate precursors, oleylamine, CTAC, glucose, and Mo(CO)6, followed by acetic acid treatment to remove surfactants and dispersion on Ketjen Black-300 carbon.. Test conditions: HER tested in N2-saturated 1 M KOH (LSV scan rate 5 mV s−1, stability via chronoamperometry at 11 mV and 10,000 CV cycles); MOR tested in N2-saturated 1 M KOH + 1 M CH3OH (CV scan rate 20 mV s−1, stability via chronoamperometry at 0.65 V and 1,000 CV cycles).. Findings: The Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst exhibits an ultrasmall overpotential of 11 mV at a current density of 10 mA cm−2 for HER, compared to 84 mV for commercial Pt/C.; The mass activity for HER is 10.96 A mg−1Pt at −0.07 V vs. RHE, significantly higher than the 0.83 A mg−1Pt of commercial Pt/C.; The catalyst achieves a mass activity of 15.04 A mg−1Pt for MOR, which is 10 times higher than that of Pt/C (1.45 A mg−1Pt).; The catalyst maintains 99% of its current density after 10 hours of chronoamperometry at 11 mV, whereas Pt/C retains only ~53%.; After 10,000 CV cycles, the Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst shows no obvious negative shift in overpotential, while Pt/C shifts by ~33 mV.; The Tafel slope for HER is 30 mV dec−1 for the HEA catalyst compared to 98 mV dec−1 for Pt/C, indicating faster kinetics.; CO stripping onset potential is 0.391 V vs. RHE for the HEA catalyst, a 181 mV decrease compared to Pt/C (0.572 V), indicating superior CO anti-poisoning.; DFT calculations reveal a low activation barrier of 0.11 eV for water dissociation and a rate-determining step energy barrier of 0.45 eV for MOR.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the performance to a synergistic effect of multi-active sites on the HEA surface, where different elements (Pt, Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) facilitate specific steps: Pt acts as an electron reservoir, Ni and Co dominate the electroactive region near the Fermi level for electron depletion, and Fe stabilizes intermediates. This configuration enables fast site-to-site electron transfer, efficient water dissociation, and optimal binding strength for intermediates, while the lattice distortion and multi-component nature inhibit CO poisoning and structural degradation.. Limitations: The text notes that slight stoichiometry variations (e.g., changing Cu content) lead to slightly lower activity, though the optimal composition is robust; it also mentions that non-noble metals (Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) may leach slightly during electrocatalysis, causing minor stoichiometry variations, although the overall structure remains stable.. Future work: The authors propose that the simple oil phase synthesis strategy and the understanding of the multi-active sites and fast site-to-site electron transfer mechanism will lay the foundation for the preparation of other HEAs and their application in related electrocatalysis.. Quote: "The Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst exhibits excellent electrocatalytic performance for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and methanol oxidation reaction (MOR)."

card: Paper card. Question: How can uniformly dispersed high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) be synthesized on granular supports (e.g., carbon, Al2O3, zeolite) without phase separation, overcoming the limitations of conventional fixed-bed pyrolysis?. System: Denary (MnCoNiCuRhPdSnIrPtAu), quinary (FeCoPdIrPt, CuPdSnPtAu), and other multi-element (up to 10 elements) HEA-NPs supported on graphene oxide (GO), carbon black, γ-Al2O3, and zeolite (Permutit). Processing: Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) following wet impregnation: Metal chlorides coordinated with 1,10-Phenanthroline loaded on supports; quartz boat pushed into a 923 K furnace zone at 20 cm s−1 (reaching 923 K within 5 s); annealing for 120 min at 923 K under Ar (100 sccm) or H2 (100 sccm) for oxide supports. Test conditions: Electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in 1 M KOH (pH 13.8) at 10 mA cm−2 and 100 mA cm−2; stability tested via chronopotentiometry for 150 h; structural characterization via HR-STEM, HAADF-STEM, EDX, XRD, XPS, and ICP-OES. Findings: HEA-NPs achieved a narrow size distribution of ~2 nm up to denary compositions at 923 K; FMBP ensures simultaneous pyrolysis of mixed precursors, preventing phase separation unlike fixed-bed pyrolysis (FBP) which yields phase-separated alloys; FeCoPdIrPt@GO exhibited an overpotential of 42 mV at 10 mA cm−2, lower than commercial Pt/C (64 mV); Mass activity of FeCoPdIrPt@GO at 100 mV overpotential was 9.1 mA μgPt, 26 times higher than Pt/C (0.35 mA μgPt); Long-term stability of 150 h maintained at 10 mA cm−2 with no obvious change in morphology or composition; Atomic ratio error in synthesized alloys was below 15%, confirmed by EDX and ICP-OES; Tafel slope for FeCoPdIrPt was 82 mV dec−1, indicating the fastest kinetics among tested samples. Mechanism: The rapid heating to 923 K within 5 s creates high supersaturation of monomers, leading to a small critical nucleus radius (r* = 0.313 nm) and low critical excess free energy (ΔGr* = 2.54 × 10−20 J). This thermodynamically favors the formation of small, homogeneous nuclei clusters without phase separation, whereas slower heating (FBP/SMBP) results in larger nuclei and phase segregation due to higher ΔGr*.. Limitations: The text notes that HEA-NPs with low loading (3 wt%) were too small for clear EDX mapping, requiring higher loading (10 wt%) for elemental analysis; also, annealing times of 30 min led to carbon wrapping, while 180 min caused significant particle growth.. Future work: The authors propose a scalable method for production of supported HEA-NPs and suggest the strategy opens a venue for synthesizing alloys with tunable compositions for applications in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion.. Quote: "Fast moving bed pyrolysis strategy ensures the mixed metal precursors rapidly and simultaneously pyrolyzed at high temperatures, resulting in nuclei with a small size."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles be synthesized at low temperatures on conventional supports, and what mechanisms govern their formation and catalytic performance in CO2 hydrogenation?. System: CoNiCuRuPd high-entropy alloy nanoparticles supported on TiO2 (CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2); comparison with CoNiCuRuPd/Al2O3, CoNiCuRuPd/MgO, and monometallic Pd/TiO2, Ru/TiO2, Co/TiO2, Ni/TiO2, Cu/TiO2. Processing: Simple impregnation of TiO2 with aqueous solutions of Co(NO3)2·6H2O, Ni(NO3)2·6H2O, Cu(NO3)2·3H2O, RuCl3·nH2O, and Na2PdCl4 (1:1:1:1:1 molar ratio; Pd 1.0 wt%); reduction under H2 flow (20 mL/min) at 400 °C for 2 h without prior calcination. Test conditions: CO2 hydrogenation at atmospheric pressure, 300–400 °C, with N2/H2/CO2 mixture (4/5/1 composition, total flow 50 mL/min, SV = 6000 mL/g/h); stability tested over 72 h; in situ XAFS and XRD under H2 at 200–400 °C; H2-TPR from 50 to 600 °C at 5 °C/min; CO-TPD and FTIR; TEM/STEM/EDX; ETEM under 300 kV electron beam; DFT and MD simulations at 900 K. Findings: CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 nanoparticles achieved an average size of 1.90 nm with a single-phase fcc structure (lattice parameter a = 3.734 Å), whereas CoNiCuRuPd/Al2O3 and CoNiCuRuPd/MgO yielded larger (6.65 and 6.73 nm), partially segregated particles.; The quinary-component precursors on TiO2 showed a single H2-TPR reduction peak at ~170 °C, indicating simultaneous reduction of all five metal ions, unlike broad peaks (130–250 °C) on Al2O3 and MgO.; CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 exhibited 2–13 times higher yield of hydrogenated products than MgO and Al2O3 supports, with 68.3% CH4 selectivity at 400 °C.; The apparent activation energy for CO2 hydrogenation on CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 was 37.7 kJ/mol, lower than 44.2 kJ/mol for Pd/TiO2.; After 72 h of reaction, CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 retained 96% of its initial activity, while Pd/TiO2 dropped to 76% and Ru/TiO2 to 89%.; Particle growth was suppressed in CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 (final diameter 2.3 nm) compared to Pd/TiO2 (final diameter 5.3 nm) after 72 h.; DFT calculations showed the cohesive energy of the HEA cluster (−3.92 eV) was higher than that of a pure Pd cluster (−3.09 eV), and diffusion coefficients in the HEA were ~1/3 lower than in pure Pd at 900 K.; CO adsorption on the HEA surface was stronger (Ead = −37.5 kcal/mol) than on pure Pd (−26.2 kcal/mol), shifting the CO stretching frequency from 2091 cm−1 (Pd/TiO2) to 2070 cm−1 (HEA/TiO2) and delaying desorption to >150 °C.. Mechanism: The formation is driven by hydrogen spillover on TiO2: Pd2+ precursors are first reduced to form Pd nuclei; H2 dissociates on Pd to form Pd–H species; protons and electrons transfer to TiO2 lattice O2− anions, generating mobile H atoms that migrate rapidly over TiO2 via coupled proton/electron transfer, reducing all metal precursors simultaneously to form a solid-solution HEA. The sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion in the HEA enhance durability, while the cocktail effect (synergistic electronic properties) improves catalytic activity and CH4 selectivity by strengthening CO adsorption.. Limitations: The study notes that the synthesis method was demonstrated only for the CoNiCuRuPd system and a few preliminary tests with Rh, Pt, and Au; applicability to other compositions requires further investigation. The text also mentions that monometallic Ru/TiO2 showed high activity but attributed it to extremely small particle size (0.89 nm), implying size effects must be controlled when comparing HEAs to monometallics.. Future work: The authors state that 'Further investigation to demonstrate the applicability of the present synthetic method is now under investigation' for other metal combinations (e.g., Rh, Pt, Au) and suggest the approach offers 'advanced insights into an innovative catalyst/photocatalyst architecture providing an essentially unlimited compositional space.'. Quote: "This process is driven by the pronounced hydrogen spillover effect on TiO2 in conjunction with coupled proton/electron transfer."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the advances in design, synthesis, and applications of high-entropy metal-organic frameworks (HE-MOFs) for catalysis and energy storage?. System: High-entropy metal-organic frameworks (HE-MOFs). Processing: Various methods, including solvothermal, hydrothermal, co-precipitation, mechanochemical synthesis, and electrodeposition. Findings: HE-MOFs have abundant active sites, stable framework structures, and adjustable chemical properties; HE-MOFs demonstrate exceptional catalytic activity and impressive electrochemical energy storage performance; The high-entropy strategy can improve the catalytic activity and stability of MOFs; HE-MOFs have potential applications in various fields, including catalysis, energy storage, and conversion. Mechanism: The high-entropy strategy can create lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, and a cocktail effect, which contribute to the attractive properties of HE-MOFs. Limitations: The current reports on the application of HE-MOFs in catalysis are limited, and more systematic studies are needed to explore the mechanism of how the high-entropy strategy enhances catalytic activity. Future work: Further research is needed to design advanced HE-MOFs with desired properties and to explore their potential applications in various fields. Quote: "HE-MOFs have garnered significant attention in the fields of catalysis and renewable energy technology"

Paper card. Question: How do high-entropy metal-organic frameworks (HE-MOFs) perform in energy storage applications?. System: Mn, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn-based Na1.19(Zn0.23Mn0.19Ni0.19Cu0.21Co0.18)[Fe(CN)6]0.81□0.19 (M5HCF), HE-PBA, HEO850. Test conditions: 0.5 C, 1 C, 0.1 C, 0.2 C, 0.5 C, 1 C, -10 to 80 °C. Findings: Average capacity of 75 mAh g−1 at 0.5 C; Capacity retention of 87% after 1000 cycles at 1 C; Specific capacity of 570.9 mAh g−1 after 200 cycles at 0.1 C; Ultra-stable cycling performance with a negligible capacity decay of 0.043% per cycle at 0.5 C after 800 cycles; Specific capacitance of 175 F g−1 at 5 mV s−1; Specific capacitance of 336 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1. Mechanism: The high-entropy strategy enables M5HCF to possess a smaller bandgap, reducing the difficulty associated with electron excitation and leading to faster diffusion kinetics. Limitations: The development of HE-MOFs is in its nascent stages, and there is still much research work that needs to be performed to achieve further progress in this field. Future work: Research on high-entropy MOFs containing six or more metal components is necessary to explore the influence of increased configurational entropy on alleviating the Jahn-Teller effect. Quote: "applying the high-entropy strategy to HE-MOFs introduces multiple metal ions into their framework structure, creating abundant redox-active sites and thereby enhancing their electrochemical performance"

card: Paper card. Question: Can an entropy-forming-ability (EFA) descriptor based on first-principles energy distribution spectra predict the synthesizability of disordered five-metal refractory carbides as homogeneous high-entropy single phases?. System: Five-metal refractory carbides (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5, HfMoTaWZrC5, HfMoTiWZrC5, HfMoVWZrC5) derived from eight metals (Hf, Nb, Mo, Ta, Ti, V, W, Zr) and carbon. Processing: Solid-state synthesis via ball milling (2 h total, 30-min intervals with 10-min rests) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2200 °C, 100 °C/min heating rate, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 5-min dwell in vacuum/argon atmosphere. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification; Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for chemical homogeneity; Nanoindentation at 27 °C ± 0.5 °C with 50 mN load for Vickers hardness (HV) and elastic modulus (E); Williamson–Hall analysis for lattice strain. Findings: The EFA descriptor correctly predicted that MoNbTaVWC5 (EFA = 125 (eV/atom)−1), HfNbTaTiZrC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1), and HfNbTaTiVC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1) would form homogeneous single phases, while HfMoVWZrC5 (EFA = 37 (eV/atom)−1) would not.; Six of the nine synthesized compositions (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5) exhibited single rock-salt fcc phases, whereas the three lowest-EFA compositions showed multiple secondary phases.; Vickers hardness of HfNbTaTiZrC5 reached 32 GPa, which is 50% higher than the rule of mixtures (ROM) prediction, and HfTaTiWZrC5 reached 33 GPa.; The Pearson correlation between the inverse EFA (EFA−1) and lattice distortion (ε) was 0.97, and the Spearman rank correlation was 0.98, validating EFA as a synthesizability descriptor.; Lattice distortion (ε) ranged from 0.063% for MoNbTaVWC5 (most homogeneous) to 0.325% for HfMoVWZrC5 (least homogeneous).; The highest-EFA composition MoNbTaVWC5 formed a homogeneous phase despite using precursors Mo2C and W2C with different structures (orthorhombic and hexagonal) and stoichiometries compared to the rock-salt product.; Vibrational contributions to formation free energy at 2000 K ranged from ~0 meV/atom to −31 meV/atom, which are significantly smaller than the configurational entropy contributions required to overcome formation enthalpy barriers (50–150 meV/atom).; A threshold of EFA ~50 (eV/atom)−1 was identified as the point above which homogeneous disordered single phases are likely to form.. Mechanism: The authors argue that a narrow energy distribution spectrum (low standard deviation σ) implies a low energy cost to access metastable configurations, promoting configurational randomness (entropy) at finite temperatures. This entropy stabilization allows the disordered rock-salt phase to remain locked in upon cooling, even when competing ordered phases exist. Enhanced hardness is attributed to mass disorder causing impedance mismatch that scatters dislocations, increasing resistance to plastic deformation.. Limitations: The study notes that the Williamson–Hall formalism does not provide particularly accurate absolute values of lattice strain (ε), though it is effective for relative comparisons. Additionally, the vibrational contribution to entropy is an order of magnitude smaller than configurational entropy, and the study did not investigate the specific effect of carbon stoichiometry on melting points.. Future work: The authors state that an investigation of the effect of carbon stoichiometry is clearly warranted to understand how vacancies might further improve high-temperature performance, although it is outside the scope of this study.. Quote: "The descriptor correctly predicts the ease with which compositions can be experimentally synthesized as rock-salt high-entropy homogeneous phases, validating the ansatz, and in some cases, going beyond intuition."

Question: How do electronegativity differences between mixed elements in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) influence charge redistribution and the specific adsorption of OH* and H* intermediates to overcome scaling relations in water splitting?. System: FeCoNiXRu (X: Cu, Cr, Mn) high-entropy alloy nanoparticles supported on carbon nanofibers (FeCoNiXRu/CNFs), specifically FeCoNiMnRu with composition Fe0.23Co0.22Ni0.22Mn0.14Ru0.19. Findings: FeCoNiMnRu/CNFs achieved the lowest overpotential of 71 mV to produce a current density of 100 mA cm−2 for HER, significantly lower than Ru/CNFs (421 mV) and FeCoNi/CNFs (410 mV).; The Tafel slope for FeCoNiMnRu/CNFs was 67.4 mV dec−1, indicating a Volmer–Heyrovsky mechanism.; DFT calculations identified the Co site as the most active center for water dissociation with the lowest energy barrier of 0.34 eV.; Ru sites exhibited the most appealing Gibbs free energy of hydrogen adsorption (ΔGH*) of −0.07 eV, making them the preferred sites for H* adsorption.; Operando Raman spectroscopy confirmed the formation of Ru-H* intermediates at 2069 and 2092 cm−1, which were absent in samples without Ru.; Decreasing the electronegativity of the fifth metal (from Cu to Mn) reduced the energy barriers for water dissociation and H* adsorption.; The FeCoNiMnRu/CNFs||FeCoNiMnRu/CNFs electrolyzer system required only 1.65 V to achieve 100 mA cm−2 for overall water splitting.; The catalyst maintained a stable current density of 1 A cm−2 for over 600 h in 1.0 M KOH without structural degradation.. Mechanism: Electronegativity differences between the mixed elements (Fe: 1.83, Co: 1.88, Ni: 1.91, Mn: 1.55, Ru: 2.20) induce significant charge redistribution, causing electron transfer from Fe, Co, Ni, and Mn to Ru. This creates highly active Co sites optimized for water dissociation (stabilizing OH*) and Ru sites optimized for H* adsorption, allowing simultaneous stabilization of multiple intermediates and breaking scaling relations.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The work opens up a fascinating direction for breaking scaling relation issues for multistep reactions by constructing controllable multifunctional active sites on HEA surfaces.. card: Paper card. Question: Can a multiobjective Bayesian optimization framework be used to discover high entropy alloy electrocatalysts with balanced catalytic activity, cost-effectiveness, and entropic stabilization in vast composition spaces?. System: High entropy alloys (HEAs) composed of up to 10 elements (Ag, Au, Cu, Ir, Os, Pd, Pt, Re, Rh, and Ru). Findings: The multiobjective BO framework can efficiently identify promising HEA electrocatalysts with balanced properties; The framework can handle high-dimensional design spaces with up to 10 elements; The identified optimal HEAs achieve a balance among catalytic activity, cost-effectiveness, and entropic stabilization; The framework is data-efficient, requiring only 50-140 evaluations to reach 95% of the maximum hypervolume indicator; The framework can be used to explore different regions of the compositional landscape and identify diverse promising candidates. Mechanism: The framework uses a diversity-guided batch selection strategy and a Gaussian process regression (GPR) surrogate model to explore the design space and predict the catalytic activity of arbitrary HEAs. Limitations: The simplified assumption of the surface model, which may not be completely accurate for describing the true catalyst surface. Future work: Improving the surface model by developing a better ML model for phase prediction and further experimental characterization. Quote: "we have developed a data-efficient multiobjective BO framework tailored for the discovery of HEA electrocatalysts for ORR"

card: Paper card. Question: What are the properties and applications of rare-earth high-entropy oxides?. System: Rare-earth high-entropy oxides (RE-HEOs). Processing: Various synthesis techniques, including solid-state reaction, sol-gel method, solution combustion synthesis, spray pyrolysis, and nebulized spray pyrolysis. Findings: 1.9; 3.0; 9.2; 0.8; 78; 97; 100; 800. Mechanism: The configurational entropy inherent in RE-HEOs reduces phase separation, ensuring durability under harsh operating conditions. Limitations: Challenges remain in scaling up production, optimizing compositions for specific applications, and understanding the fundamental mechanisms governing their multifunctionality. Future work: Further research is needed to explore the potential of RE-HEOs in various applications, including energy conversion and storage, catalysis, and environmental remediation. Quote: "Rare-earth high-entropy oxides are a new promising class of multifunctional materials"

Paper card. Question: How can rare-earth high-entropy oxides (RE-HEOs) be utilized for CO2 reduction and other applications?. System: Rare-earth high-entropy oxides (RE-HEOs), such as (Ce0.2Zr0.2La0.2Nd0.2Sm0.2)O2−δ and Ce0.5(LaPrSmY)0.5O2−y. Processing: Anchoring method, including adsorption of rare-earth metal cations by negative functional groups on the surface of graphene oxide, refluxing for 4 h at 170 °C, and calcinating at temperatures over 500 °C. Test conditions: Photocatalytic conditions, high temperature and high pressure for thermal catalysis, and electrocatalytic conditions with an external electric field. Findings: RE-HEOs demonstrated significant catalytic performance for CO2 conversion under photocatalytic conditions; Achieved a production of 14.4 mol CO kg−1 h−1 and 1.27 mol CH3OH kg−1 h−1 with high selectivity for CO and methanol; Fluorite RE-HEOs showed tunable bandgap range of 2.0–3.5 eV, making them suitable for photovoltaic and LED applications; RE-HEOs exhibited enhanced thermal shock resistance and oxidation durability, making them suitable for high-temperature applications; High-entropy zirconate-based oxides maintained their structural integrity under high-radiation exposure and exhibited stable luminescent performance. Mechanism: The catalytic performance of RE-HEOs is linked to their defect chemistry, particularly the formation and stabilization of oxygen vacancies. Limitations: Current synthesis methods are not scalable and energy-efficient, and the high cost of rare-earth elements is a potential barrier to commercialization. Future work: Development of advanced synthesis techniques, investigation of less commonly studied rare-earth elements, and exploration of hybrid systems integrating RE-HEOs with other functional materials. card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and high-entropy oxides (HEOs) be synthesized and applied as protective layers for interconnectors and anode components in hydrocarbon-fueled solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) to overcome issues like chromium evaporation and carbon deposition?. System: FeCoNiMnCu high-entropy alloy coating converted to (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel; HEA/GDC anode catalyst containing Ni, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn on Gd-doped CeO2 (GDC) support. Processing: Vacuum induction melting to create sputtering target; magnetron sputtering deposition of 4 μm coating on SUS 430 steel at 200 °C for 2 h (1.2 kW power, 0.13 Pa Ar); thermal conversion at 800 °C for 10 weeks (1680 h total); co-precipitation of HEA from nitrate precursors with citric acid, calcination at 500 °C for 6 h, mixing with GDC (65:35 wt ratio). Test conditions: Oxidation in air at 800 °C for up to 10 weeks; SOFC cell testing at 750 °C; Steam reforming of methane (SRM) in fixed-bed tube reactor at 700–800 °C with GHSV of 45,000 1/h. Findings: After 10 weeks of oxidation at 800 °C, the FeCoNiMnCu coating converted to a uniform (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel layer with a surface Cr concentration of only 4.34%.; The area-specific resistance (ASR) of the oxidized HEA coating decreased from 8.21 mΩ·cm² after 1 week to 6.59 mΩ·cm² after 10 weeks at 800 °C.; The ASR of the scale was 17 mΩ·cm² at 600 °C, which is well below the accepted limit of 0.1 Ω·cm².; The HEA/GDC catalyst showed excellent stability during SRM, whereas Ni/YSZ and Ni/GDC catalysts rapidly degraded with time.; After 30 h of SOFC cell testing, the post-test HEA/GDC anode layer was carbon-free, while the Ni/YSZ anode contained 17.3% carbon.; The reforming rate of the HEA/GDC catalyst increased from 27% at 700 °C to 42% at 800 °C.; A current density of approximately 100 mA/cm² was achieved at 750 °C in the SOFC cell test using the HEA/GDC anode.. Mechanism: The high-entropy spinel coating thermally converted from the HEA effectively blocks chromium out-diffusion from the substrate, reducing the growth of the Cr-rich oxide layer and lowering electrical resistivity. The HEA-based anode demonstrates superior carbon resistance because the mingled sites of multiple transition metals prevent the deposition and fiber growth of carbon that typically damages Ni-based anodes.. Limitations: The conductivity of the (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel was not measured directly in the study; the reforming rate of the HEA/GDC catalyst was lower than that of the Ni-based catalysts at 750 °C.. Future work: Further study and development of carbon-resistant anodes for hydrocarbon-fueled SOFCs with direct internal reforming is needed based on the promising results.. Quote: "The coating of 4 μm in thickness was deposited on the SUS 430 steel substrate under sputtering power of 1.2 kW for 2 h at 200 °C in a chamber with an Ar pressure of 0.13 Pa."

Paper card. Question: How does high configurational entropy and multi-cation doping affect the ionic conductivity, activation energy, and structural stability of fluorite- and pyrochlore-structured high-entropy oxides (HEOs) compared to conventional SOFC electrolytes like YSZ and GDC?. System: Fluorite-structured HEOs: (Hf0.25Zr0.25Ce0.25Y0.25)O2-δ (HEFO1), (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ce0.2)(Y0.2Yb0.2)O2-δ (HEF04B), (Hf0.327Ce0.456Zr0.217)0.85Yb0.15O1.93 (Yb-15(1)); Pyrochlore-structured HEOs: (Nd0.2Sm0.2Gd0.2Dy0.2Y0.2)2Zr2O7 (HEC-1 to HEC-5); Ceria-based HEOs: CeGdDySmPrO2-δ, CeGdLaSmPrO2-δ. Processing: High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering and annealing in air at 1500 °C with furnace cooling (50 °C/min); Solid-state reaction method with final sintering at 1500–1700 °C; Sol-gel method followed by compaction and free sintering at 1500 °C in air. Test conditions: Electrical conductivity measured in dry air in the temperature range of 650–850 °C; Conductivity measured at 600 °C and 800 °C; Activation energy determined in temperature ranges of 300–750 °C and 170–560 °C. Findings: Conductivity of fluorite HEOs (e.g., HEFO1) at 850 °C ranged from 1.9 to 2.9 mS/cm, significantly lower than the 30 mS/cm observed for YSZ.; Activation energies for HEO fluorites were 1.14–1.29 eV, higher than the 1.0 eV for YSZ.; The highest conductivity for ZrO2-based HEOs (CCFO2) was 5.35 × 10−4 S/cm at 600 °C with an activation energy of 0.66 eV.; Pyrochlore HEC-5 achieved a conductivity of 7.1 × 10−3 S/cm at 800 °C, higher than base low and medium zirconates.; Ceria-based HEOs (CeGdLaSmPrO2-δ) reached 0.001 S/cm at 510 °C with activation energies of 0.52–0.53 eV.; Increasing the cation radius ratio r(A3+)/r(B4+) in pyrochlore HEOs increased conductivity due to higher mobile vacancy concentration.; Raman spectroscopy showed a blue shift in the main band for HEOs, indicating lattice compression, and an increase in the 570 cm−1 band intensity indicating more oxygen vacancies.. Mechanism: The authors argue that ionic conductivity in HEOs is inhibited by local crystal lattice distortion caused by relatively high ionic radius differences (δrion), which lowers oxygen mobility. Additionally, high deviation of oxygen non-stoichiometry from the optimal 4% value leads to defect association, reducing free charge carriers. In pyrochlore structures, higher conductivity is ensured by a continuous and energetically favorable pathway for oxygen jumps between 48f-sites, which cannot form in fluorite structures due to random cation/anion occupation.. Limitations: The high cost and limited resources of scandium and gallium in alternative electrolytes; poor chemical stability of Bi2O3-based electrolytes in reducing atmospheres; reduction of Ce4+ to Ce3+ in doped ceria under anode conditions causing power efficiency loss; difficulty in stabilizing fluorite HEOs without deterioration of transport properties; low conductivity of HEOs compared to conventional electrolytes in many cases.. Future work: Further efforts should be applied to the search for new methods to stabilize fluorite HEOs without deterioration of their transport properties; HEOs with pyrochlore structure are highly stable and entropy disordering enhances transport properties, providing a point for future development; HEO proton and dual conductors with perovskite structure are highly demanded.. Quote: "The authors argue that decreasing the conductivity may be related to a smaller gran size of HE ceramics as well as to a high doping level, exceeding the optimal value for the ZrO2-based ceramic equal to 8–10 mol.%"

card: Paper card. Question: What are the mechanisms of fatigue crack initiation and propagation in high-entropy alloys?. System: High-entropy alloys, including CrCoFeMnNi, Al0.5CoCrFeNi, and Al0.7CoCrFeNi. Test conditions: Cyclic loading, rotating bending fatigue test, and tensile test at room temperature and low temperature. Findings: Slip is one of the main mechanisms of crack initiation in high-entropy alloys; The presence of high-entropy configurations leads to a higher likelihood of dislocation formation along parallel slip planes; The fatigue performance of high-entropy alloys is significantly influenced by both inherent defects within the alloy and defects introduced during processing; The introduction of a multi-component B2 phase with ductility and transformability into high-entropy alloys can improve fatigue life; The combination of ultrafine grain and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) can increase fatigue resistance. Mechanism: The authors propose that the mechanisms of fatigue crack initiation and propagation in high-entropy alloys are related to slip, dislocation formation, and the presence of defects. Limitations: The authors note that the study of fatigue behavior in high-entropy alloys is still in its early stages and more research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms. Future work: The authors propose that future research should focus on systematically studying the fatigue strength of high-entropy alloys under various loading conditions and investigating the effect of environmental conditions on fatigue performance. Quote: "Slip is one of the main mechanisms of crack initiation in the CrCoFeMnNi alloy"

card: Paper card. Question: Is polymorphism still possible in entropy-stabilized high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that are generally believed to possess extremely high structural stability and maintain a single-phase structure?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (Cantor's alloy). Processing: Synthesized via gas-atomization (melt injected into high purity Ar at 4 MPa pressure); subjected to hydrostatic compression up to ~41 GPa using a diamond anvil cell (DAC) with helium as pressure-transmitting medium; subsequently heated using resistive heating (up to 723 K) or double-sided Nd:YLF laser heating (up to ~1,400 K) at various pressures (6, 14, 26 GPa).. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to ~41 GPa; heating at ambient pressure up to 723 K; heating at 6, 14, and 26 GPa up to ~1,400 K; in situ synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring.. Findings: The fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transition starts at approximately 22 GPa and almost completes at approximately 41 GPa.; The phase transition is irreversible; the hcp phase is retained when pressure is released to ambient conditions.; The hcp phase remains stable up to 633 K at ambient pressure before transforming back to fcc.; At 26 GPa, the critical temperature for the hcp-to-fcc transition is approximately 1,400 K.; The isothermal bulk modulus (B0) is 153.9±3.0 GPa for the fcc phase and 150.2±4.6 GPa for the hcp phase.; The c/a ratio of the hcp phase remained almost constant at 1.62±0.01 during compression and decompression.; The transition is sluggish, with fcc and hcp phases coexisting over a wide pressure range of ~22 to ~41 GPa.; Decompression from different maximum pressures yields fcc/hcp composites with tunable fractions.. Mechanism: The transition occurs because the hcp structure is thermodynamically more favorable at lower temperatures and high pressures, while the fcc phase is stable at higher temperatures and lower pressures; the transition is kinetically hindered by high energy barriers and low stacking fault energy (~20 mJ m−2), requiring high pressure to overcome these barriers to form the hcp phase.. Limitations: The transition is sluggish and irreversible, making it difficult to determine the real equilibrium phase boundary (Clapeyron coexistence curve) experimentally; grain size was not small enough for statistically reliable Rietveld refinement of volume fractions; overshooting often exists due to high energy barriers.. Future work: The authors suggest that this behavior could be general in various HEAs and propose new avenues for tailoring HEA properties via polymorphic transition-induced HEA composites, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where transition pressure could be largely decreased.. Quote: "The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: How can fatigue life be enhanced in high-entropy alloys at low strain amplitudes without sacrificing ductility, specifically by addressing the trade-off between fatigue strength and fatigue-crack-initiation resistance in precipitation-strengthened alloys?. System: Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy containing an FCC matrix and multicomponent B2 precipitates (NiAl-type). Processing: Vacuum-induction melting to fabricate a large plate, followed by hot rolling with 60% reduction at 1150 °C, and annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Monotonic tension at RT with a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; fully-reversed strain-controlled low-cycle fatigue (LCF) at RT with strain amplitudes from ±0.1% to ±1.75% and a strain rate of 1 × 10−2 s−1; real-time in situ neutron diffraction at strain amplitudes of ±0.5%, ±1%, and ±1.75%. Findings: The alloy exhibits at least four times longer fatigue life than conventional alloys at a plastic strain amplitude of ~0.03%.; The B2 phase bears significantly more stress than the FCC phase after yielding, with lattice strains nearly ten times larger.; Stress-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) occurs in the B2 phase, evidenced by abnormal peak broadening and peak separation in neutron diffraction.; Deformation twinning is observed in the FCC matrix only at high strain amplitudes (≥1.75%), not at intermediate amplitudes (1%).; The B2 phase is plastically deformable at all tested strain amplitudes, storing dislocations and relieving stress concentration.; Fine B2 precipitates act as efficient crack arresters, forming blunted cracks, whereas coarse band-like B2 precipitates initiate microcracks.; The multicomponent B2 phase has lower antiphase boundary (APB) energies (e.g., compared to 0.697 eV/m² for pure NiAl) enabling plastic deformation.. Mechanism: The enhanced fatigue life is attributed to the ductile-transformable character of the multicomponent B2 precipitates, which undergo reversible martensitic transformation and plastic deformation to accommodate strain incompatibility with the FCC matrix. This mechanism relieves stress concentration at phase boundaries, retards microcrack initiation, and provides alternative deformation pathways, unlike brittle traditional intermetallics.. Limitations: The study notes that if the B2 phase size is too large (e.g., band-like precipitates), it becomes easy to initiate microcracks due to longer incoherent interfaces where stress concentration cannot be effectively accommodated.. Future work: The authors propose that the design strategy of introducing ductile-transformable multicomponent intermetallic precipitates can guide the design of fatigue-resistant alloys by tuning HEA compositions and thermomechanical processing.. Quote: "the current HEA shows at least four times longer life than conventional alloys"

card: Paper card. Question: How can noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials be synthesized with precise control over their composition and crystal structure, and what is the role of noble metals in their formation?. System: Noble metal-based high-entropy alloys (NM-HEAs) with compositions including Pt, Ir, Ru, Pd, Fe, Cu, Ni, and Co. Processing: Spray drying technique combined with thermal decomposition-reduction (SD-TDR) method, with parameters including heating rate of 3°C/min, thermal decomposition temperature of 300°C, and cooling rate of 5° to 10°C/min. Test conditions: Methanol oxidation reaction (MOR) performance tested in an aqueous solution of 0.5 M H2SO4 and 0.5 M CH3OH. Findings: The synthesized PtNiCoCuRuIr HEA-3DNF demonstrates exceptional MOR performance, with a mass activity of 2637 mA/mgPt; Noble metals (Pt, Ru, and Ir) play a crucial role in facilitating the reduction of Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe by generating highly reactive hydrogen atoms on their surfaces; The phase composition of NM-HEA-3DNF can be precisely controlled by adjusting the reduction temperature and Pt-to-Ru atomic ratio; A phase transition from Pt-based fcc structures to Ru-based hcp structures can be achieved within PtNiCoCuRu HEA-3DNF; The SD-TDR method allows for the synthesis of NM-HEA nanomaterials with a 3DNF structure and single-phase solid solution. Mechanism: The noble metals (Pt, Ru, and Ir) facilitate the reduction of Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe by generating highly reactive hydrogen atoms on their surfaces, leading to the formation of single-phase solid solution alloys. Future work: Further research is needed to explore the applications of NM-HEA nanomaterials in various catalytic fields and to develop more efficient and targeted material design. Quote: "Noble metal–based high-entropy alloys (NM-HEAs) are promising catalysts because of their diverse compositions and complex surface structures"

W2999482379.title: High-Entropy Alloys as Catalysts for the CO 2 and CO Reduction Reactions

card: Paper card. Question: How do the unique structural features of compositionally complex solid solutions (CCSS) enable new concepts in electrocatalyst design compared to traditional catalysts, and what are the strategies to exploit these features for activity, selectivity, and stability?. System: Compositionally complex solid solutions (CCSS) and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) defined as single-phase solid solutions with five or more elements, including specific examples like Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and Pd-based systems.. Processing: Synthesis via entropy-driven routes at high temperatures or high energies to ensure negative Gibbs free energy; non-equilibrium methods such as fast cooling rates (quenching) to kinetically trap metastable phases or achieve high deviations from equiatomic compositions (e.g., 60–70% of one element).. Test conditions: Electrochemical reactions including oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), oxygen evolution reaction (OER), hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), CO oxidation, CO reduction, CO2 reduction, NH3 synthesis/decomposition, MeOH oxidation, EtOH oxidation, and Li-O2 batteries.. Findings: CCSS materials form a single-phase solid solution where all elements are statistically distributed, creating millions of different multielement active sites with a continuous distribution of binding energies.; The binding energy distribution pattern (BEDP) for a quinary alloy shows at least five distinct binding peaks, with the position of the peak maximum related to overpotential and the integral related to the number of active sites.; Increasing the molar ratio of a specific element can increase the number of sites within a binding peak to about 60–70%, significantly surpassing the loss of site probability compared to unary catalysts.; In CCSS surfaces, the scaling relation between *O and *OH/*OOH is broken because *O binds at threefold hollow sites while *OH and *OOH bind at on-top sites with different elemental compositions.; For cascade reactions like CO2 reduction, the multifunctionality allows intermediate products to desorb and re-bind at different sites, enabling the synthesis of higher-carbon products.; The thermodynamic stability of the CCSS phase is counterbalanced by kinetic stabilization due to sluggish diffusion and high solid diffusion barriers, leading to high electrocatalytic stability.; The position of individual elements in standard volcano plots is not decisive; for example, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni showed good ORR activity even though all individual elements are far from optimal volcano positions.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the immense flexibility in adjusting binding energies arises because every active site has a different elemental environment due to the statistical distribution of elements. This creates a continuous coverage of binding energies via BEDP peak broadening, allowing the formation of sites with ideal binding energies. Additionally, the unique multifunctionality allows different reaction steps or intermediates to bind at different sites, breaking traditional scaling relations and enabling cascade reactions.. Limitations: A lower abundance of relevant active sites on the surface compared to unary catalysts; the complexity of predicting suitable element combinations due to multielement interactions; challenges in synthesizing particles with controlled composition, size, and morphology; and the potential for thermodynamic degradation if the CCSS phase is metastable.. Future work: The authors propose developing a database summarizing calculated and experimental data, implementing high-throughput methods, using machine learning tools to identify trends in the complex composition space, and designing synthesis routes that allow upscaling to industrial scale while controlling electrochemical properties.. Quote: "Since the binding energy is a result of many short‐range and long‐range interactions of the binding atom(s) with all neighbouring atoms, an active site can consist of any possible arrangement of the constituent elements."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a high-throughput technique be developed for combinatorial compositional design and rapid synthesis of ultrafine multimetallic nanoclusters with a homogeneous alloy structure?. System: PtPdRhRuIrFeCoNi. Processing: Thermal shock heating (∼1,650 K, ∼500 ms) of precursor-loaded carbon support. Test conditions: Electrochemical screening using scanning droplet cell and rotating disk electrode setup in 0.1 M KOH and 1 M KOH. Findings: Ultrafine and homogeneous alloy MMNCs can be synthesized using thermal shock heating; The MMNCs exhibit a single-phase FCC structure; Two promising catalysts (PtPdRhNi and PtPdFeCoNi) were identified and verified using RDE setup; The MMNCs show higher activity and stability compared to Pt control sample; The high-throughput synthesis and screening method can accelerate compositional exploration for MMNC study. Mechanism: The high-temperature synthesis in the multielement samples with a high entropy largely drives the alloy formation. Limitations: The complexity of multielement systems limits the interpretation of the high performance of the two compositions. Future work: Data mining and machine learning can be used to uncover the hidden relationships on the elemental contributions to the catalytic performances. Quote: "High-throughput, combinatorial synthesis of multimetallic nanoclusters"

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing the configurational disorder (number of first-row transition metals) in spinel oxides affect CO oxidation activity and long-term stability compared to lower entropy variants?. System: Spinel oxides (M3O4) with M = Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn; specifically 4-metal (CrMnFeCo)3O4, 5-metal (CrMnFeCoNi)3O4, 6-metal (CrMnFeCoNiCu)3O4, and 7-metal (CrMnFeCoNiCuZn)3O4. Processing: Solventless thermolysis of equimolar metal diethyldithiocarbamate precursors dissolved in dichloromethane, heated to 900 °C (15 °C min−1 ramp rate) in static air, and held for 4 h. Test conditions: Plug-flow reactor, total flow 50 mL min−1, feed gas 1 vol.% CO, 5 vol.% O2, Ar balance; temperature ramp 50 to 650 °C at 10 °C min−1; stability test held for 14 h at temperatures below T50 (e.g., 208 °C for 7-metal). Findings: The 7-metal HESO showed a T10 value of 168 °C, which was a 63% decrease compared to the 4-metal MESO (454 °C).; The 7-metal HESO exhibited a T50 value of 250 °C, which was 56% lower than the 5-metal HESO (569 °C).; During 14 h of operation, the 7-metal spinel oxide showed a decrease in activity of only 4.7% ± 0.3%, whereas the 4-metal variant decreased by 12.2% ± 0.4%.; The 7-metal HESO saw an improvement in CO conversion with a rate of +0.62 ± 0.13% h−1 between 0 and 2 h, while the 4-metal spinel oxide decreased at −0.85 ± 0.07% h−1.; Rietveld refinement determined the lattice parameter for the 7-metal HESO as 8.33 Å, decreasing as the number of metals increased.; A minor monoclinic CuO secondary phase (5.0 ± 0.3 wt.%) was observed in the 6- and 7-metal samples.; Post-catalysis XPS showed the ratio of the second oxygen environment (OB, M-OR/OV) to lattice oxygen (OA) decreased for all samples, but the 6- and 7-metal HESOs maintained higher ratios than lower entropy systems.. Mechanism: The authors propose that adding cations that prefer tetrahedral sites (Ni, Cu, Zn) drives multi-valent, catalytically active metals (Mn, Fe) out of tetrahedral sites and into octahedral sites, which are more prevalent at the surface. Additionally, higher disorder correlates with an increase in oxygen vacancies, which helps regulate the generation of reactive oxygen species in catalytic oxidation reactions proceeding via the Mars–van Krevelen mechanism.. Limitations: The study was conducted under dry conditions; industrially realistic feeds containing catalyst poisons such as sulfur and water are known to cause significant deactivation and were not tested. Some Cr segregation was observed at the nanoscale, and a small amount of CuO secondary phase formed in the 6- and 7-metal samples.. Future work: Ongoing operando investigations of more complex reactions (such as Fischer-Tropsch), synchrotron-based cation distribution analysis, and testing with realistic reaction feeds containing catalyst poisons such as water.. Quote: "A substantial 63% decrease in the T10 value (temperature to reach 10% CO oxidation) is observed by systematically increasing the number of first‐row transition metals within the spinel oxide."

card: Paper card. Question: How does entropy stabilization in transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) influence reversible lithium storage capacity, cycling stability, and the underlying reaction mechanism compared to medium entropy oxides?. System: Transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) with composition (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O; compared to 4-cation medium entropy oxides (MEO) such as (Co0.25Cu0.25Zn0.25Ni0.25)O and (Co0.25Cu0.25Mg0.25Zn0.25)O. Processing: Nebulized Spray Pyrolysis (NSP) at 1150 °C; 4-cation systems required post-annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h under ambient atmosphere; electrodes cast with 63 wt% active material, 22 wt% Super C65, 15 wt% PVA binder. Test conditions: Galvanostatic cycling in Li-metal coin cells, voltage range 0.01–3 V vs. Li+/Li, specific currents from 50 to 3000 mA g−1, room temperature, 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC or EC/EMC electrolyte. Findings: The 5-cation TM-HEO cycled over 300 cycles at 200 mA g−1 with specific capacities stabilizing around 650 mAh g−1 after initial activation.; The 5-cation system achieved a specific capacity of 770 mAh g−1 after 100 cycles following a rate increase to 3 A g−1 for 5 cycles.; Medium entropy oxides (4-cation systems) showed rapid capacity degradation, with the Co-removed variant failing completely after ~10 cycles.; The Coulombic efficiency of the 5-cation TM-HEO stabilized between 99.4% and 99.95% in the range of cycles 60–400.; The 4-cation system without Zn (TM-MEO(-Zn)) exhibited a two-step oxidation process at 1.7 V and 2.2 V, unlike the single-step oxidation of the 5-cation system.; High-loading electrodes (2.3 mg cm−2) maintained Coulombic efficiencies >98.5% and an areal capacity of 1.3 mAh cm−2 after 30 cycles.; No metallic phases or Cu dendrites were detected via TEM/EDX after 100 cycles, despite the conversion reaction mechanism.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the rock-salt structure is preserved as a permanent host matrix during the entire conversion process. While some cations (e.g., Co, Cu) are reduced to metallic states during lithiation, they remain 'trapped' within the defect-rich rock-salt lattice stabilized by unreduced cations (e.g., Mg, Ni). This entropy stabilization lowers the Gibbs free energy, favoring the re-incorporation of reduced cations into the original lattice sites upon delithiation, preventing phase separation and structural collapse.. Limitations: The theoretical capacity cannot be predicted with high accuracy due to unknown additional processes like Zn-Li alloying or intermetallic formation; some 4-cation systems (TM-MEO(-Mg) and TM-MEO(-Ni)) could not be synthesized as single-phase compounds even at high temperatures.. Future work: Further investigations should be pursued to explore the full potential of high entropy oxide electrode materials, including the addition of other cations (Fe, Mn, Cr, V) to develop a modular method for tailoring electrodes to specific needs.. Quote: "The stabilization effect of entropy brings significant benefits for the storage capacity retention of high entropy oxides and greatly improves the cycling stability."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy solid solutions be formed in non-oxide ceramic metal diborides with a hexagonal layered structure, and do they exhibit superior hardness and oxidation resistance compared to their constituent individual diborides?. System: Seven equimolar five-component metal diborides: (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Mo0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Mo0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Cr0.2Ti0.2)B2, and (Hf0.2Zr0.2W0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2. Processing: High-energy ball milling (HEBM) for 6 hours in WC media with 60-minute milling/5-minute cooling cycles, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under 30 MPa pressure in vacuum (10^-2 Torr). Test conditions: Hardness measured via Vickers indentation at 200 kgf/mm2 with 15s hold time; oxidation resistance assessed via sequential isothermal annealing in flowing dry air at 800–1500 °C for 1 hour per step. Findings: Six of the seven compositions formed a single-phase hexagonal AlB2 structure with greater than 92% of theoretical density.; Aberration-corrected STEM confirmed 2-D high-entropy metal layers separated by rigid boron nets with no detectable layered segregation along the c-axis.; The measured standard deviations of lattice spacings between basal (0001) planes were only ~0.6% of the average c lattice parameter.; Hardness of the high-entropy diborides was generally greater than the average hardness of the five individual constituent metal diborides.; Oxidation resistance was generally better than the average of individual components, with HEB#1 and HEB#7 maintaining shape at 1500 °C while TiB2 pulverized.; Revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factors based on lattice constants (δc) of 3.9% to 5.2% rationalized single-phase formation, whereas the non-single-phase specimen had δc ≈ 6.2%.; Minor secondary oxide phases ((Zr, Hf)O2) were observed in six specimens, and a secondary (Ti1.6W2.4)B4 phase was found in the W-containing specimen.. Mechanism: The formation of high-entropy solid solutions is rationalized by a revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factor calculated from lattice constants rather than atomic radii; the rigid 2-D boron net constrains the metal layers, reducing the effective size mismatch (δa) and allowing entropy stabilization of the disordered solid solution despite larger atomic size differences in the c-direction.. Limitations: The presence of porosity and oxide inclusions resulting from the HEBM procedure adversely affected hardness and oxidation resistance; MoB2 is metastable at room temperature and W2B5 starting powder has limited solubility; the study did not fully optimize microstructure for maximum property performance.. Future work: Further systematic investigation of hardness, oxidation resistance, and other properties is needed, particularly focusing on processing optimization to achieve fully-dense and oxide-free specimens and utilizing the large compositional design space to tailor protective oxide scales.. Quote: "Greater than 92% of the theoretical densities have been generally achieved with largely uniform compositions from nanoscale to microscale."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high entropy oxide materials be designed to be water-resistant and exhibit excellent catalytic performance?. System: High entropy oxide materials, specifically (Ni0.2Mg0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2Co0.2)Cr2O4. Processing: Mechanochemical method using ball milling, followed by calcination at 550 °C for 2 h. Test conditions: C3H6 oxidation reaction in dry and humid conditions (4.2 vol% H2O). Findings: High entropy oxide materials exhibit better water resistance and catalytic performance compared to single metal oxides; The (Ni0.2Mg0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2Co0.2)Cr2O4 material shows excellent water resistance (>100 h) in C3H6 oxidation; The material has a lower T90 (265 °C) compared to single metal oxides (318-350 °C) in dry conditions; The material exhibits weak H2O adsorption ability and strong hydrothermal stability; The material has a lower formation energy of oxygen vacancies, which improves its catalytic performance. Mechanism: The high entropy structure of the material leads to a lower Gibbs free energy, which enhances its stability and water resistance. The material's surface has a weaker H2O adsorption ability, which reduces the competitive adsorption with C3H6 and improves its catalytic performance.. Future work: Further exploration of the capabilities of high entropy oxide materials in heterogeneous catalysis and the development of new materials for water-resistant catalysis. Quote: "Herein, a concept of engineering entropy to design water-resistant oxide catalysts is proposed"

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy materials be used to improve the performance of advanced batteries?. System: High-entropy alloys, high-entropy oxides, and high-entropy MXenes. Findings: High-entropy materials have exceptional properties such as remarkable structural stability, enhanced ionic conductivity, superior mechanical strength, and outstanding catalytic activity; High-entropy alloys can simultaneously enhance both strength and ductility, and prolong strain hardening; High-entropy oxides demonstrate superior properties, including excellent mechanical strength, enhanced structural and high-temperature stability, as well as a notable magnetocaloric effect; High-entropy MXenes have unique hydrophilicity, conductivity, and redox pseudocapacitance, and have garnered significant attention in the field of energy catalysis; High-entropy materials have been successfully employed as cathode, anode, and electrolytes in batteries, demonstrating remarkable cycling performance and high specific capacity. Mechanism: The underlying mechanisms can be attributed to four core effects of HEMs: high-entropy effect, lattice distortion effect, sluggish lattice diffusion effect, and cocktail effect. card: Paper card. Question: How does compositional heterogeneity affect the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles?. System: Fe18Co16Ni8Cu20Pd12.5Ir1.5Pt10Au14 nanoparticles. Processing: Fast Moving Bed Pyrolysis (FMBP) strategy, with a heating rate of 10 K·min−1 and annealing at 923 K for 120 min. Test conditions: In situ compression testing in a transmission electron microscope (TEM) with a displacement control rate of 2 nm·s−1. Findings: The yield strength of HEA nanoparticles exhibits a transition from a “smaller-is-stronger” to a “smaller-is-weaker” phenomenon below a critical size of ~180 nm; The deformation mode changes from homogeneous to heterogeneous with decreasing particle size; The work-hardening ability deteriorates significantly below the critical size; The compositional heterogeneity leads to a variation in local stacking-fault energy (SFE) and lattice friction; The critical size for the transition is influenced by the spatial correlation length of compositional heterogeneity. Mechanism: The compositional heterogeneity 'roughens' the landscape for dislocation motion, leading to a variation in local SFE and lattice friction, which in turn affects the mechanical properties. Limitations: The experimental results are limited to a specific alloy composition and processing route. Future work: Further studies are needed to explore the effect of compositional heterogeneity on the mechanical properties of HEAs with different alloy compositions and processing routes. Quote: "compositional heterogeneity plays an important role in affecting the mechanical properties of HEAs"

card: Paper card. Question: How can a novel, cost-effective synthesis strategy for high-entropy metal phosphides be developed to overcome sluggish lithium polysulfide (LiPS) conversion kinetics and the shuttle effect in Li–S batteries?. System: Fe0.20Co0.62Ni0.14Cu0.23Mn0.38P nanoparticles anchored on a porous carbon network (HEP/C); comparative systems include Fe0.38Co0.75Ni0.20Cu0.36P/C (MEP/C), Fe2P/C, and Mn2P/C. Processing: One-step thermal treatment of cation-bonded phosphate resin precursors containing Fe3+, Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, and Mn2+ ions; the process involves thermally induced transformation to form single-phase nanoparticles uniformly dispersed on porous carbon. Test conditions: Li–S batteries tested at 0.2C (initial capacity 1402.18 mA h g−1), 5C (1000 cycles with 0.05% decay), and high sulfur loadings of 5.0–9.0 mg cm−2; symmetric cells used Li2S6 electrolyte with CV at 1 mV s−1; pouch cells operated at 0.05C with 8.1 mg cm−2 sulfur loading. Findings: HEP/C delivered an initial specific capacity of 1402.18 mA h g−1 at 0.2C, significantly higher than MEP/C (1133.3), Mn2P/C (978.4), and Fe2P/C (1027.7) mA h g−1.; The HEP/C@S cathode exhibited a capacity decay rate of 0.05% per cycle over 1000 cycles at 5C.; HEP/C achieved the lowest peak-to-peak separation (ΔE) of 89.8 mV in symmetric cells, indicating fast redox kinetics.; The HEP/C@S cathode showed the lowest Tafel slope of 182 mV dec−1 in LSV measurements compared to 306 mV dec−1 for MEP/C.; DFT calculations revealed HEP (002) exhibited the strongest Li2S6 adsorption energy among tested catalysts.; The HEP/C@S cathode achieved a QL/QH ratio of 2.6, indicating superior polysulfide conversion kinetics.; A practical pouch cell with 8.1 mg cm−2 sulfur loading delivered an energy density of 455 Wh kg−1.; Atomic-resolution STEM revealed lattice strains of 0.1% tensile and 0.1% compressive strain due to atomic radius mismatches.. Mechanism: The catalytic improvements arise from synergistic electronic modulation by the five constituent metals, which elevates d-band electron energy levels (to -0.71 eV), and lattice distortion induced by atomic radius mismatches (e.g., Cu vs. Mn), collectively generating a dense array of highly active catalytic sites that enhance LiPS adsorption, lower energy barriers for conversion, and facilitate Li+ transport.. Limitations: The text notes that Mn2P exhibits a high energy barrier during the critical step of Li2S2 conversion to Li2S, hindering nucleation and growth; Fe2P/C shows high capacity decay due to poor adsorption; MEP/C and Mn2P/C show low cycling capacities due to poor activation of S and LiPS conversion.. Future work: The authors state the work presents an efficient synthesis strategy and provides fundamental insights into the design principles of advanced LiPS conversion catalysts, implying future application in high-performance Li–S batteries, but do not explicitly list specific future experiments.. Quote: "For the first time, we successfully fabricated single-phase high-entropy Fe0.20Co0.62Ni0.14Cu0.23Mn0.38P nanoparticles anchored on a porous carbon network (HEP/C)."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the halogen-induced p-band center regulation affect the performance of lithium-sulfur batteries?. System: Cs2SnX6 (X = Cl, Br, I) halide perovskites. Processing: Hydrothermal method, followed by ball-milling to reduce particle size. Test conditions: Room temperature, various current rates (0.2-5C), high sulfur loading (6.1 mg cm−2), low electrolyte/sulfur ratio (5.5 μL mg−1), and wide temperature range (−20 to 50 °C). Findings: The p-band center of halogen anions shifts positively toward the Fermi level with increasing halogen atomic number; Cs2SnI6 exhibits the highest electrical conductivity and electrocatalytic activity among the three samples; The Cs2SnI6 battery shows a high initial capacity of 1000 mA h g−1 at 2C and a low decay rate of 0.068% per cycle after 500 cycles; Cs2SnI6 achieves a remarkable reversible capacity of 768.8 mA h g−1 at a high sulfur loading and low E/S ratio; The Cs2SnI6 battery exhibits excellent cycling stability and rate performance, even at extreme temperatures. Mechanism: The halogen-induced p-band center regulation enhances the electron transfer ability and strengthens the binding energy between Cs2SnI6 and LiPSs, leading to improved adsorption and catalytic performance. Quote: "the p-band center of halogen anions shifted positively toward the Fermi level with the increase in the halogen atomic number"

Paper card. Question: How do halogen-induced p-band centers regulate the adsorption and catalytic performance of lithium–sulfur batteries?. System: Sn-based halide perovskites, specifically Cs2SnI6. Test conditions: 2C, 5C, 0.1C at −20 °C, 0.5C at 50 °C. Findings: High discharge capacity (1000 mA h g−1 at 2C); Excellent rate performance (771.0 mA h g−1 at 5C); Long-term cycle stability (0.068% decay rate per cycle after 500 cycles at 2C); High discharge capacity at extreme temperatures (912.7 mA h g−1 at 0.1C at −20 °C and 1350.7 mA h g−1 at 0.5C at 50 °C). Mechanism: The p-band center of the halogen anion shifts positively toward the Fermi level as the atomic number of the halogen increases, resulting in a higher charge transfer rate and promoting the kinetics of the conversion reaction of LiPSs. Quote: "the regulatory mechanism of halogen-induced p-band centers and their effects on the adsorption and catalytic performance of LSBs were successfully explored"

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy materials (HEMs) leverage configurational entropy to overcome the limitations of conventional enthalpy-dominated catalysts, specifically regarding phase stability, active site tunability, and the breaking of scaling relationships in electrocatalysis?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) including PtPdCoNiFeCuAuSn, PtPdRhRuCe, Ru0.44Rh0.30Co0.12Ni0.14, CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10, IrPdPtRhRu, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, and AlNiCoIrM; High-entropy oxides (HEOs) and perovskites; Multimetallic nanoclusters (MMNCs).. Processing: Carbothermal shock (ultrafast joule heating followed by rapid quenching at ~1500 K); Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) reaching 923 K within 5 s; Colloidal synthesis with seed-mediated coreduction and annealing at 600°C; Ionic liquid-assisted cosputtering; Ball milling and solvothermal synthesis.. Test conditions: Ammonia oxidation at 700°C; Ammonia decomposition at 500°C; Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in acidic and alkaline media; Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in acidic and alkaline media; Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in acidic and alkaline solutions; Li-O2 battery cycling.. Findings: Quinary HEA nanoparticles (PtPdRhRuCe) achieved ~100% conversion and >99% selectivity toward NO + NO2 at 700°C with no degradation over 30 hours.; HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst reached a mass-specific rate of 0.74 gNH3 m−2 hour−1 at 500°C, representing improvement factors of ~24 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~19 versus Ru.; Computational models predicted an IrPdPtRhRu HEA composition with a ~40-mV lower overpotential relative to Pt (111) for ORR.; Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni nanoparticles with size less than 2 nm delivered ORR activity comparable to Pt under the same conditions.; Octonary RuIrCeNiWCuCrCo catalyst outperformed quaternary and binary counterparts in long-term operation for Li-O2 batteries due to higher configurational entropy.; GO-supported quinary HEA nanoparticles (FeCoPdIrPt) exhibited enhanced HER activity and stability in alkaline solutions relative to commercial Pt/C catalysts.; HEA catalysts containing five or more elements outperformed binary, ternary, and quaternary alloys in alkaline media due to broad adsorption energy distributions.. Mechanism: Enhanced configurational entropy stabilizes single-phase solid solutions despite large enthalpic differences, allowing atomic mixing of multiple principal elements. Severe lattice distortion lowers the energy barrier for adsorption and activation, while the diverse local coordination environments and electronic perturbations (ligand effects) create a near-continuum distribution of adsorption energies. This distribution allows the catalyst to access optimal binding strengths for intermediates, breaking the linear scaling relationships that limit conventional catalysts.. Limitations: Low surface area of bulk HEAs limits catalytic utilization; maintaining nanoscale morphology at elevated temperatures is difficult due to migration and aggregation; synthesis of single-phase HEAs requires overcoming thermodynamic barriers; characterization is challenging due to increased compositional and structural complexities; phase segregation can occur if entropy is insufficient to overcome enthalpic differences.. Future work: Further elucidation of structure-property relationships across different HEM subcategories; development of high-throughput synthesis and measurement tools for accelerated materials discovery; deeper mechanistic studies on surface restructuring under reaction conditions; optimization of catalyst stability for noble metal-free applications.. Quote: "The ability to confine multiple principal elements in a single lattice is intriguing for the design of advanced catalysts with desirable activity, selectivity, and stability."

Paper card. Question: How can the configurational entropy in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be leveraged to overcome the miscibility limitations of traditional alloys and enhance catalytic performance for complex reactions like ethanol oxidation?. System: Platinum-group metal (PGM) high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles containing Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir, and Pt; specifically compared against physical mixtures of unary PGMs and binary/ternary/quaternary/quinary PGM alloys.. Processing: Prepared using a facile polyol method to synthesize PGM-HEA nanoparticles.. Test conditions: Electrochemical ethanol oxidation reaction in aqueous solution; performance compared against commercial Pd/C, Pd black, Pt/C, and Au@PtIr/C catalysts; cyclic voltammetry used to analyze individual constituent contributions.. Findings: The PGM-HEA nanoparticles exhibited much higher activity relative to commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts.; Negligible activity was observed for the physical mixture of the six unary PGM nanoparticles, confirming the necessity of atomic mixing.; The PGM-HEA delivered a mass activity more than 1.5 times higher than that of the most active catalyst to date (Au@PtIr/C).; The PGM-HEA exhibited the highest current density in the full potential range compared to ternary, quaternary, and quinary PGM alloys.; Pt and Pd are active for ethanol conversion but become poisoned by adsorbed (CO)ad or CHx species.; Os and Ru facilitate the oxidation of (CO)ad, mitigating the poisoning effect for Pt and Pd.; Ir and Ru ensure that dehydrogenation or C─C cleavage occurs at a low potential, while further oxidation hinges on Pt and Pd components.. Mechanism: The atomically mixed metals in HEAs play distinct yet concerted functions: Pt and Pd drive ethanol conversion; Os and Ru mitigate poisoning by oxidizing adsorbed species; Ir and Ru lower the potential for C─C cleavage and dehydrogenation. This synergy allows for efficient and complete oxidation of ethanol involving multiple proton-electron transfers.. Limitations: The text notes that while simple reactions can be triggered by mono- and bimetallic PGMs, it is difficult to drive complex reactions involving multiple proton-electron transfers and intermediate species without the synergistic effects provided by HEAs.. Future work: The authors imply the need to better understand the contribution of each metal to the overall reaction, as demonstrated by their comparison of cyclic voltammetry curves of individual constituents to elucidate specific roles in preventing poisoning and facilitating cleavage.. Quote: "The PGM-HEA nanoparticles efficiently catalyzed the ethanol oxidation reaction, exhibiting a much higher activity relative to that of the commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: How do multiple metal-nitrogen bonds affect the activity and durability of high-entropy alloy electrocatalysts?. System: N-doped high-entropy alloy (HEA) electrocatalyst with a Pt-rich shell and a N-doped PtCoFeNiCu core on a carbon support (denoted as N–Pt/HEA/C). Processing: thermal annealing process and an acid-etching de-alloying strategy. Test conditions: rotating disk electrode (RDE) testing in 0.1 M HClO4 aqueous solution, membrane electrode assembly (MEA) testing in HDV applications. Findings: The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst showed a high mass activity of 1.34 A mgPt–1 at 0.9 V for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR); The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability in both RDE and MEA testing; The formation of multiple metal–nitrogen bonds improved the corrosion resistance of the 3d transition metals and enhanced the ORR durability; The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst exhibited a more positive half-wave potential (E1/2) of 924 mV than Pt/HEA/C and commercial Pt/C; The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst showed a high current density of 1437 mA cm–2 at 0.7 V and only 18 mV drop at 0.8 A cm–2 after 30,000 voltage cycles. Mechanism: The enhanced ORR activity of N–Pt/HEA/C originated from the optimized adsorption energy of intermediates, resulting in the tailored electronic structure formed upon N-doping. Quote: "Multiple Metal–Nitrogen Bonds Synergistically Boosting the Activity and Durability of High-Entropy Alloy Electrocatalysts"

card: Paper card. System: High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) and High-Entropy Nanomaterials (HENMs). Processing: Various methods including mechanical alloying, dealloying, pulsed laser ablation, sputtering deposition, electrodeposition, hydrothermal synthesis, and solvothermal method. Findings: HEAs and HENMs exhibit enhanced catalytic activity due to their unique properties such as high-entropy effect, lattice distortion effect, sluggish diffusion effect, and cocktail effect; HEAs can be designed to have optimized composition and structure for improved catalytic performance; HENMs have been demonstrated as efficient electrocatalysts for various reactions including oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), oxygen evolution reaction (OER), hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), and carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR); HEAs and HENMs show improved stability and durability compared to traditional catalysts; Computational methods such as density functional theory (DFT) can be used to screen and design HEAs and HENMs for improved catalytic performance. Mechanism: The high-entropy effect, lattice distortion effect, sluggish diffusion effect, and cocktail effect contribute to the enhanced catalytic activity of HEAs and HENMs. Future work: Further research is needed to explore the potential of HEAs and HENMs for advanced electrocatalysis and to overcome the challenges associated with their synthesis and application. Quote: "HEMs have tremendous potential as electrocatalysts due to the synergistic effects of various elements"

Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy nanomaterials be used as electrocatalysts for advanced energy conversion applications?. System: 2D high‐entropy transition metal dichalcogenides, (MoWVNbTa)S2, Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27, PGM–HEA, PdPtCuAgAu, RuFeCoNiCu, PtPdRhRuCe. Processing: chemical vapor transport method, liquid‐phase exfoliation, synthesis of uniform NPs. Test conditions: CO2 reduction at different potentials, alcohol oxidation reaction in 1.0 m KOH solution with 1.0 m ethanol, nitrogen reduction reaction, ammonia oxidation reaction. Findings: Up to −0.31 V versus RHE, the FE of CO formation was over 90%; PGM–HEA showed a much higher j specific value in comparison to single platinum group metal NPs; PdPtCuAgAu NWs showed the largest mass activity and the lowest onset potential among other Pd‐based metal nanocatalysts; RuFeCoNiCu/CP showed a low overpotential (0.05 V vs RHE) and high FE (38.5%) for NRR; PtPdRhRuCe NPs exhibited ≈100% conversion of ammonia and >99% selectivity toward nitrogen oxides. Mechanism: The enhanced catalytic activity of HENMs is explained by the cocktail effect, and the d‐band center of the alloy and the absorption energy are related to electrocatalysis. Limitations: There are still fundamental and practical issues of HENMs as electrocatalysts to be considered, such as moderate synthesis strategies, structural control, optimization of element combination and composition, and reaction mechanism. Future work: Developing an advanced synthetic approach, unveiling the relationship between the properties of HENMs and the catalytic activity, and discovery of reaction mechanisms. Quote: "Beyond metal alloys, 2D HEMs are getting attention because of their large surface area"

Findings: Microhardness increased by 37.6% compared to LM13 alloy; Compressive strength increased by 73.3% compared to LM13 alloy; Tensile strength increased by 47.8% compared to LM13 alloy; Wear rate decreased with increasing sliding velocity beyond 1.5 m/s; Applied load is the most significant parameter affecting wear rate, followed by sliding distance and sliding velocity. Mechanism: The addition of HEA particles refines the grain structure, increases dislocation density, and enhances solid solution strengthening, leading to improved mechanical properties and wear resistance. Limitations: High cost of producing ball-milled HEA with uniform particle size, limited to dry sliding wear conditions. Future work: Optimizing the composite for real-world applications, exploring behavior under lubricated and high-temperature environments. card: Paper card. Question: How does a dual-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure in an equiatomic AlCrFeNiV high-entropy alloy influence its hardness and wear resistance under dry and lubricated sliding conditions?. System: Equiatomic AlCrFeNiV high-entropy alloy (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni, V). Processing: High-energy ball milling (SPEX 8000 mill, 2 h, ball-to-powder ratio 10:1, argon atmosphere) followed by spark plasma sintering (1100 °C for 1 h, 40 MPa axial pressure) and furnace cooling. Test conditions: Vickers hardness (5 N load, 15 s hold); reciprocating sliding wear against Al2O3 balls (10 N load, 0.18 m s−1 sliding speed, 30 min duration) under dry and lubricated (deionized water) conditions at ambient temperature. Findings: Hardness reached 1076 ± 15 HV0.5, significantly higher than previously reported values.; The microstructure consists of two BCC phases: BCC1 (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni) and BCC2 (enriched with 61.9 at.% V and Cr).; Average grain size was measured at 450 nm.; Wear rate under dry conditions was 17.2 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1.; Wear rate under lubricated conditions was 12.4 × 10−5 mm3 N−1 m−1.; Average coefficient of friction (COF) was 0.34 in dry conditions and 0.15 under lubrication.; Hertzian contact stress at 10 N load was calculated to be 1887 MPa.; Oxygen content on the worn surface in dry friction was 2.2 at.% higher than in lubricated friction.. Mechanism: The superior hardness and wear resistance are attributed to solution strengthening from the mixture of two different BCC systems, high-density grain and phase boundaries acting as barriers to dislocation movement, and the inhibitory effect of the hard BCC2 phase on grain boundary movement and plastic flow. The wear mechanism involves abrasive wear, delamination, and oxidation, where a dense but locally unstable oxide layer forms and fractures, while the tight binding between BCC1 and BCC2 inhibits interfacial crack formation.. Limitations: The authors note that while hardness is very high, the plasticity of the alloy is poor, making the surface prone to fracture and generating fragments that can cause a secondary grinding effect and increase wear rates.. Future work: The authors suggest that the strategy of combining high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering is beneficial for developing new materials applicable in cutting tools.. Quote: "The hardness of the AlCrFeNiV alloys reached 1076 ± 15 HV0.5."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of CoCrCuFeTi High Entropy Alloy (HEA) as a reinforcement through Friction Stir Processing (FSP) affect the tribological behavior of Stainless Steel (SS304)?. System: CoCrCuFeTi High Entropy Alloy (HEA) reinforced SS304. Processing: Friction Stir Processing (FSP) with a tungsten carbide tool rotating at 1000 rpm, traverse speed of 25 mm/min, and a load of 10 kN, followed by annealing at 650 °C for 2 h. Test conditions: Pin-on-disc wear test with varying load (10-40N), sliding velocity (0.5–3.5 m/s), and sliding distance (500–2000 m). Findings: The processed sample with HEA after annealing offered 29.8%, 57.4%, and 58.49% improved wear resistance at the minimum level of load, sliding velocity, and sliding distance than the processed base samples; The worn surface morphology revealed delamination, abrasion, adhesion, and oxide layer formation as the predominant wear mechanisms; The addition of HEA particles induced dislocation and hindered grain growth, leading to improved microhardness and wear resistance. Mechanism: The authors propose that the improved wear resistance is due to the synergistic effect of the ultrafine refined grains by the FSP process and the stress relieved microstructures after annealing, as well as the dislocation-strengthening mechanism involved in the process. Quote: "The processed samples exhibited excellent refinement in grains with uniform HEA reinforcement distribution"
